Empirical Research Plan: “Bank Durability and Borrower Outcomes”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Borrower-level staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) / event-study that compares the evolution of borrower outcomes before and after the first observable moment of “severe bank distress” (closure, FDIC intervention, official prompt-corrective‐action, or regulatory capital breach) for borrowers whose main bank is affected, versus otherwise‐similar borrowers whose main bank remains sound over the same calendar time.

Why appropriate?
• Bank distress arrives at different dates for different banks → staggered timing delivers quasi-experimental variation.  
• Borrowers are plausibly “as good as randomly” exposed to the shock once we difference‐out borrower fixed effects and common time shocks.  
• Institution lends itself to pre-period placebo (parallel-trend) tests and rich event-time dynamics.

Optional enhancement: Propensity-score / nearest-neighbor matching on pre-event borrower and bank characteristics to tighten comparability; plus re-weighting (Callaway-Sant’Anna or Sun-Abraham estimators) to address heterogeneous treatment timing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable (T_ib):  
T_ib = 1 if borrower i’s primary lender b experiences a distress event in quarter τ and t ≥ τ (post-period).  
Primary lender is defined as the bank with the highest share of outstanding credit to the borrower in the last fiscal year before τ.

Control Group:  
Borrowers whose primary lenders never enter distress during the sample window OR have not yet entered distress by calendar date t. They form the counterfactual path of outcomes absent a shock to bank durability.

Treatment Timing:  
Event time k = t – τ (e.g., k = –4,…,+8 quarters). A borrower can transition from control to treatment once; afterwards it is always treated.

Key variation: Cross-sectional exposure to failing vs. non-failing banks and the staggered calendar timing of each failure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (Conditional): In the absence of distress, borrowers connected to soon-to-fail banks would have evolved like comparable borrowers tied to stable banks.  
Plausibility: Testable with pre-event coefficients; matching on bank & borrower fundamentals improves credibility.

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Spillovers): Outcomes for control borrowers are not directly affected by other banks’ failures.  
Plausibility: Reasonable when borrowers borrow locally and banking markets are segmented, but needs checks for regional credit-supply spillovers.

A3. No Anticipatory Effects: Borrower outcomes do not change before the event because of perfect foresight of impending failure.  
Plausibility: Short pre-period anticipatory behavior may occur; examine leads in event study.

A4. Relationship Persistence: Borrower’s main lender is correctly identified and remains dominant in the immediate post-event period (at least until the shock hits).  
Plausibility: Many relationships are “sticky,” yet we will test robustness to alternative lender‐definition windows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selection / Omitted Borrower Risk  
• Riskier borrowers may self-select into weaker banks.  
Mitigation: (i) Borrower fixed effects in panel DiD capture time-invariant risk; (ii) matching on pre-event observable risk; (iii) placebo pre-trends.

T2. Credit-Market Spillovers  
• Regional credit crunch may hit even control borrowers, violating SUTVA.  
Mitigation: Include region-by-time fixed effects (e.g., county×quarter) and, in robustness, drop borrowers in the same commuting zone as a distressed bank.

T3. Measurement Error in “Primary Lender”  
• If lender classification is noisy, attenuation bias may arise.  
Mitigation: Construct lender share from regulatory call reports matched to loan schedules; re-run analysis restricting to borrowers with ≥70 % exposure to one bank.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)           # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(EventStudy)       # optional; Sun-Abraham / CS estimators
library(MatchIt)          # matching
# ---------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ---------------------------------------------
# Borrower-level panel (firm_id, year_qtr, outcome vars, etc.)
borrowers <- read_csv("borrower_panel.csv")

# Bank distress events (bank_id, distress_qtr)
events <- read_csv("bank_distress_events.csv")

# Lender–borrower mapping (firm_id, bank_id, credit_share, year_qtr)
mapping <- read_csv("lender_share.csv")

# ---------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------
# identify primary lender by highest share in t-1
primary <- mapping %>% 
  group_by(firm_id, year_qtr) %>% 
  slice_max(credit_share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  select(firm_id, year_qtr, bank_id_primary = bank_id)

# merge data sets
panel <- borrowers %>% 
  left_join(primary, by = c("firm_id","year_qtr")) %>%
  left_join(events, by = c("bank_id_primary" = "bank_id")) 

# Calculate event time (quarters from distress)
panel <- panel %>% 
  mutate(event_time = as.integer(year_qtr) - as.integer(distress_qtr),
         treated = if_else(!is.na(distress_qtr) & year_qtr >= distress_qtr,1,0))

# Keep observations with clear exposure
panel <- panel %>% filter(!is.na(bank_id_primary))

# ---------------------------------------------
# 3. Baseline DiD Specification
# Y_ity = α_i + γ_t + β*Treated_it + ε_it
# ---------------------------------------------
did_reg <- feols(outcome ~ treated | firm_id + year_qtr, data = panel, cluster = ~bank_id_primary)
summary(did_reg)

# ---------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study (Sun & Abraham)
# ---------------------------------------------
# create relative time dummies, omit k = -1
panel <- panel %>% 
  filter(event_time >= -4 & event_time <= 8) %>%
  mutate(rel_time = factor(event_time))
es_reg <- feols(outcome ~ i(rel_time, ref = -1) | firm_id + year_qtr,
                data = panel, cluster = ~bank_id_primary)
iplot(es_reg)       # visualize leads/lags

# ---------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness Check: Matched Sample
# ---------------------------------------------
# pre-event borrower × bank controls for matching (size, leverage, ROA, bank capital)
pre_event <- panel %>% 
  filter(event_time == -1) %>% 
  select(firm_id, treated, size, leverage, roa, bank_tier1)

match <- matchit(treated ~ size + leverage + roa + bank_tier1,
                 data = pre_event, method = "nearest", ratio = 1)

matched_ids <- data.frame(firm_id = match$match.matrix %>% rownames())
panel_matched <- panel %>% semi_join(matched_ids, by = "firm_id")

did_match <- feols(outcome ~ treated | firm_id + year_qtr,
                   data = panel_matched, cluster = ~bank_id_primary)
summary(did_match)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that the sudden loss of a stable banking relationship tightens borrowers’ credit constraints, lowers investment, and depresses growth. Thus:

Sign(β) : Negative for investment, sales, employment, and market valuation; positive for borrowing costs.  
Magnitude: For small-to-medium enterprises, a 1-year post-failure drop of ≈5–10 % in capital expenditure and ≈3–6 % in sales would be consistent with prior crisis evidence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = concern)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(1) Credible counterfactual / parallel trends …………………… 0.8  
(2) No spillovers / SUTVA ………………………………………   0.6  
(3) Correct treatment timing & definition ……………………… 0.9  
(4) No anticipatory effects ……………………………………… 0.7  
(5) Measurement accuracy of key variables ………………… 0.8  

Overall, the strategy is fairly strong but hinges on parallel trends and the absence of widespread spillovers; these receive focused empirical scrutiny in the analysis.
